body.text: Molly Meldrum, the former host of Countdown, has died aged 83.
For decades, if Meldrum urged viewers to "do yourself a favour" and buy your record, you knew you had made it in the music business.
Meldrum was a highly influential figure in Australia's music industry as a critic, producer, interviewer and television presenter.
The former Countdown host died peacefully this morning, his management company said.
"He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him," Profile Talent Management said in a statement.

As the host of the ABC's music show Countdown, he brought the world's biggest pop stars into people's homes, and recorded some of the most iconic — if sometimes chaotic — interviews ever broadcast on Australian television.

Instantly recognisable in his trademark cowboy hat, Meldrum was described by some as "the most important person in pop", whose influence on the chart success of performers — particularly Australians — could not be overstated.
The ABC spoke to a close friend of Molly Meldrum's who said he had been in a Melbourne hospital for a number of days before dying.
From country beginnings to the centre of the pop world
Ian "Molly" Meldrum was born in Orbost, in regional Victoria, on January 29, 1943.
He spent the first 10 years of his life in the small country town before moving to the even smaller country town of Quambatook to live with his grandmother.
"My grandmother was one of my biggest influences on my life and I lived a fair bit with her and I absolutely adored my grandmother," he said.
"She taught me one of the great things that I've tried to live my life by and she told me that no-one's above you and no-one's below you and you should treat all people as equal."
Meldrum's interest in music surged when The Beatles toured Australia in 1964, taking the country by storm.
Meldrum and his friend Ronnie Burns — who would later have a successful recording career of his own — were kicked out of The Beatles' concert in Melbourne for being "too enthusiastic".

Just a few years later, Meldrum, who had been writing for Go-Set magazine and working on local TV shows, relocated to London to document Australian band The Groop's attempts to crack the UK music scene.
It was there that he got the scoop that took his career to a new level, securing an interview with John Lennon during which the Beatle dropped the bombshell that the band was splitting up.
"The story later went worldwide on radio, in Rolling Stone, everywhere," Meldrum said in 1981.
Meldrum had also been learning the ropes as a music producer, assisting with the recording of music by artists such as The Masters Apprentices.
In 1969 he produced Russell Morris's recording of The Real Thing, transforming the song, which was written by Johnny Young as an acoustic ballad, into a six-minute, effects-laden epic.
The song was a number one hit domestically and is widely regarded as a milestone in music production in Australia.
Countdown took Molly into every home in Australia
Meldrum had experience as a television music reporter, but taking a job with brand new ABC music show Countdown was to be the single most important move in his career.

The show's executive producer, Michael Shrimpton, told the ABC in 2003 that he and a fellow producer were meeting in a Melbourne pub to discuss who to hire as the show's talent scout when Meldrum drove up onto the footpath outside.
He was initially hired as the show's talent coordinator, but progressed to an on-air role presenting a music news and review segment.
Countdown was an instant hit, capitalising on the lack of other prime-time music TV shows while being one of the first Australian programs recorded in colour.

The arrival of Countdown coincided with the emergence of music videos, making the show the ideal place for local and international acts to promote their new music — usually on Meldrum's "Humdrum" segment.
Meldrum's influence was summed up by his promotion of Abba's Mamma Mia, which was not even considered as a single by the group until Meldrum plugged it repeatedly on Countdown.
The song was number one in the Australian charts for 10 weeks and went on to become a worldwide hit.

Rather than telling viewers to go out and buy an album — which was against the ABC's policy around direct endorsements — Meldrum would tell viewers to "do yourself a favour". It became his iconic catchphrase.
Even Molly's 'stuff-ups' were magic television
It was said that electricity consumption would spike when Countdown was on air because practically every teenager in Australia switched on their TV sets.
Holding the attention of the nation's youth made Countdown, and Meldrum, extremely influential on what music made an impression on the charts.
That also gave Meldrum access to some of the biggest stars in pop music and he would have been the first to admit that some of the resulting interviews were not exactly from the live TV textbook.
But what Meldrum lacked in polish, he more than made up for in knowledge and pop music credibility.
One of his most iconic interviews was not with a pop star at all, but with a future king.
Meldrum interviewed then Prince Charles on Countdown in 1977 and — in his own words — "stuffed up" badly, fumbling his way through an introduction while the bemused royal watched on.

Meldrum dropped a few "f-bombs" and even committed a royal faux pas by touching the prince, but in the process created a priceless moment in Australian television history — one that Charles himself remembers well.
"There is an old show business saying which warns never to work with animals or children, but nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum," now King Charles recounted in 2014.
Life after Countdown
Even after Countdown ended in 1987, Meldrum was still in demand as a TV music authority, hosting a regular segment on Hey Hey It's Saturday.
He also started his own record label, Melodian Records, producing albums for Indecent Obsession, Jo Beth Taylor and Peter Andre.
Meldrum received an ARIA for special achievement in 1993 and was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014.
He was inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame in 2012, with tributes from pop stars such as Elton John and Delta Goodrem.
"I know I speak for many artists and music lovers around world when I say, 'Thank you. There's no-one like you,"
Elton John said.
Meldrum was described as "the single most important person in the Australian pop industry for 40 years" in the book 1001 Australians You Should Know.
"He's a very giving and sharing person and he's done so much for the music business," Australian music promoter Michael Chugg said.
"He's loved by everybody. He's just a wonderful person and a true Aussie icon."
More than just a hat and a catchphrase
A serious fall at his Melbourne home in 2011 left Meldrum critically injured with a fractured skull and in a coma.
The passionate St Kilda Football Club fan recovered, but later said the fall made him realise he was not bulletproof.
His colourful life was made into a successful Channel Seven TV mini-series in 2016.
In an interview with Andrew Denton on Enough Rope, Meldrum explained that his passion for music was just one aspect of his life.
"Molly Meldrum, I guess, is the image or the person or whatever that has been on Countdown, has been on Hey Hey [It's Saturday]," he said.
"Whereas there is the other side of Molly Meldrum which is the Ian Meldrum, [and] I take things very, very seriously.
"I have an intense interest in politics. I'm sort of apolitical in one sense, but I follow it religiously. I'm addicted all the time to say, BBC World News or CNN. And there is those two sides."

Several public outings in 2023, including one in which he bared his naked backside to the crowd at an Elton John concert, may have threatened to tarnish his image in later life, but Meldrum took it in his stride.
"Elton might have been singing The B*tch is Back but it was more a case of The Idiot is Back," he told The Herald Sun.
He may have been accident prone and unpolished at times, but nobody with Meldrum's gift for picking a hit song could ever be called an idiot.
